title: BEFORE YOU CALL YOURSELF A CHRISTIAN, PAUL SAYS TO TEST THIS
paragraphs: BEFORE YOU CALL YOURSELF A CHRISTIAN, PAUL SAYS TO TEST THIS
“Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith.” — 2 Corinthians 13:5
There is a Bible verse that can make even a confident Christian suddenly uncomfortable.
Not because it says God does not love you.
Not because it says you have sinned too many times.
Not because it announces that grace has run out.
It asks something far more personal.
Are you actually in the faith?
Not, “Do you attend church?”
Not, “Were you baptized?”
Not, “Do you know Christian language?”
Not, “Did you once walk down an aisle, raise your hand, repeat a prayer, or have an emotional experience?”
Paul turns the question toward the person reading his words and says:
“Examine yourselves.”
The Greek of 2 Corinthians 13:5 begins:
Ἑαυτοὺς πειράζετε εἰ ἐστὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει
Heautous peirazete ei este en tē pistei.
Literally, the force is:
Test yourselves as to whether you are in the faith.
Then Paul intensifies it:
ἑαυτοὺς δοκιμάζετε
heautous dokimazete—
prove, examine, test yourselves.
And then comes the question beneath every other question:
ἢ οὐκ ἐπιγινώσκετε ἑαυτοὺς ὅτι Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν;
“Or do you not recognize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?”
And Paul adds the sobering qualification:
εἰ μήτι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστε
—unless indeed you fail the test.
That is not comfortable Christianity.
That is apostolic Christianity.
And before you run away from the discomfort, understand why Paul said it.
The Corinthians had been demanding proof that Christ was speaking through Paul.
So Paul turned the examination around.
You want proof?
Then examine yourselves.
Paul was not inventing a spiritual torture chamber where sincere believers spend every night wondering whether one forgotten sin has erased their salvation.
He was confronting a church filled with serious problems and challenging professing believers to stop merely examining the messenger and begin examining themselves.
That distinction matters.
Because biblical self-examination is not the same thing as obsessive self-condemnation.
The purpose is not to stare at yourself until you lose sight of Jesus.
The purpose is to discover whether the Jesus you profess is truly the Jesus upon whom you depend.
And that is where this verse becomes terrifyingly relevant.
Because it is possible to become extremely familiar with Christianity without being transformed by Christ.
Judas walked beside Jesus.
He heard teachings from the mouth of Jesus Himself.
He witnessed miracles.
He participated in ministry.
He carried responsibility among the disciples.
And yet proximity to Jesus was not the same thing as belonging to Jesus.
That should disturb every version of Christianity built entirely on appearances.
You can know worship songs and still love your sin.
You can repost Scripture and refuse to forgive.
You can defend biblical morality publicly while feeding secret lust privately.
You can cry during worship and remain cruel at home.
You can own five Bibles and rarely obey the words inside them.
You can speak passionately about revival while refusing to repent.
You can serve in ministry because you love being needed.
You can preach because you love being heard.
You can give because you love being praised.
You can look alive to everybody watching you while something inside you is quietly dying.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is this:
You can become skilled at convincing other people that you know Jesus while never asking whether your life shows that Jesus knows you.
That is why examination matters.
But examination must be biblical.
Paul does not say, “Examine yourselves to determine whether you have ever struggled.”
If struggling disqualified Christians, Peter would have been finished.
He does not say, “Examine yourselves to see whether you have achieved sinless perfection.”
The apostle John explicitly warns believers against claiming sinlessness, while also teaching that those born of God cannot make peace with an ongoing life characterized by sin and rebellion.
The question is not whether sin has ever wounded your life.
The question is whether you have made peace with the weapon.
There is a difference between falling into sin and building a house there.
There is a difference between temptation and surrender.
There is a difference between a believer crying, “Lord, deliver me,” and a religious person saying, “Lord, leave this part of my life alone.”
A Christian may fall terribly.
David did.
Peter did.
The Corinthians themselves were evidence of how messy sanctification could become.
But grace does something astonishing to a person who belongs to Christ.
It makes sin increasingly impossible to call home.
You may stumble.
You may bleed.
You may have seasons where your prayers sound more like groaning than victory.
You may find yourself returning to God ashamed of something you swore you would never do again.
But somewhere beneath the wreckage remains this Spirit-produced cry:
Jesus, I don't want to live without You.
That cry matters.
Because the evidence of saving faith is not that you became impressive.
It is that Christ became indispensable.
Maybe this article is touching the thing you hoped nobody would mention.
The hidden browser history.
The bitterness you have renamed “boundaries.”
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The money controlling you.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The jealousy disguised as concern.
The unforgiveness you keep justifying.
The secret conversations.
The double life.
The addiction.
The coldness.
The prayerlessness.
The exhausting performance of looking spiritually healthy while your private relationship with God is starving.
Do not hide now.
The most dangerous response to conviction is not tears.
It is defensiveness.
Scripture says:

“Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!”
—Psalm 139:23
David does not ask God to admire his heart.
He asks God to search it.
Then:

“And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!”
—Psalm 139:24
That is the posture.
Not:
“God, prove I am better than them.”
But:
“God, expose whatever is keeping me from You.”
This is where Christianity becomes more than a label.
Because genuine self-examination eventually brings you to the humiliating realization that you cannot save yourself.
You cannot repent perfectly enough to purchase salvation.
You cannot perform enough good works to erase your guilt.
You cannot become moral enough to make the cross unnecessary.
You cannot examine yourself into heaven.
The examination reveals the disease.
Jesus is the Savior.
That distinction is everything.
Paul's command is not an invitation to replace faith in Christ with faith in your spiritual performance.
The gospel announces something infinitely better.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
Christ reigns.
And the sinner who turns to Him in repentant faith is not told to clean himself sufficiently before approaching the cross.
He comes because he cannot clean himself.
The scandal of grace is that Jesus does not wait for respectable people.
He saves sinners.
Paul himself understood this.
He had once persecuted the church of God.
He carried religious credentials while fighting against the very Messiah he thought he was serving.
Then Christ met him.
Everything changed.
That is what Jesus does.
He takes persecutors and makes them apostles.
He takes deniers like Peter and restores them.
He takes the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, greedy, drunkards, revilers, and swindlers—and after naming those realities without softening them, Paul tells the Corinthians:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then comes grace:

“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11
That single word—were—contains an entire resurrection.
Such were some of you.
Your past can tell the truth about where you have been without being permitted to dictate where Christ is taking you.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin did not matter.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because the blood of Jesus speaks a better word over repentant sinners than their worst chapter ever could.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old pages never existed.
He redeems the story.
So examine yourself.
When Scripture confronts you, do you bend—or immediately begin explaining why it does not apply to you?
When you sin, do you hide from God indefinitely—or eventually run wounded and ashamed toward the mercy of Christ?
Is Jesus useful to your lifestyle, or is Jesus Lord over it?
Do you want freedom from sin—or merely freedom from sin's consequences?
Would you still follow Christ if Christianity brought you no applause, no audience, no status, no prosperity, and no social advantage?
If nobody knew you were praying, would you still pray?
If nobody saw you giving, would you still give?
If nobody congratulated you for serving, would Jesus still be enough?
And here is perhaps the hardest question:
If Jesus told you to surrender the one thing you desperately do not want Him touching...
would you still call Him Lord?
Do not answer quickly.
Some questions deserve silence.
Because there may be something in your heart right now whispering:
Anything but that.
That relationship.
That habit.
That resentment.
That secret.
That ambition.
That identity.
That hidden compromise.
Anything but that.
Yet Jesus never recruited admirers.
He called disciples.
He said:

“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.”
—Matthew 16:24
Christianity is not adding Jesus as an accessory to the life you already planned.
It is dying with Christ and discovering that the life He gives is infinitely better than the one you were desperately trying to protect.
But perhaps another person reading this is experiencing something different.
You genuinely love Christ.
You hate your sin.
You repent.
You trust Him.
Yet 2 Corinthians 13:5 frightens you because every examination becomes another reason to believe you are hopeless.
Then hear the other side of biblical truth.
The answer to weak faith is not stronger faith in yourself.
It is looking again to a strong Savior.
Jesus said:

“Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.”
—John 6:37
The gospel does not say:
“Whoever comes to Jesus after becoming sufficiently impressive will be accepted.”
It says whoever comes.
Your assurance ultimately rests not in the perfection of your grip upon Christ but in the perfection of the Christ upon whom your faith rests.
The same Peter who denied Jesus three times was restored by Jesus.
The resurrection did not erase Peter's scandal from history.
It transformed its meaning.
Peter's failure became the place where grace demonstrated that failure does not have to have the final sentence.
Perhaps yours does not either.
Maybe you have been avoiding Jesus because you think returning after everything you have done would make you a hypocrite.
No.
Pretending you do not need Him is hypocrisy.
Returning because you desperately need mercy is repentance.
Come back.
Come filthy.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come without speeches.
Come without pretending.
But come repentant.
Come believing.
Come to Christ.
There is still blood sufficient for sinners.
There is still mercy for the broken.
There is still restoration for prodigals.
There is still forgiveness at the cross.
There is still resurrection after graves.
There is still grace after scandal.
And there is still a Savior whose name is Jesus.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already brought you from a place you once thought you would never escape, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed before deciding not to give up.
Do it to support the spread of the Gospel—not to purchase God's favor.
God cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
But if you genuinely want to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one expression of generosity.
Not because clicking “Share” proves you are saved.
But because if Christ has given us truth worth living for, then it is truth worth carrying to somebody else.
One believer may be secretly drowning.
One prodigal may believe they have wandered too far.

One unbeliever may have never understood that Christianity is not a museum for people pretending to be righteous but a proclamation that guilty sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Let them hear.
Not your pastor.
Not your spouse.
Not the hypocrite who hurt you.
Not the Christian influencer who disappointed you.
Not the church member whose life you have been criticizing.
You.
“Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith.”
Then, after examining yourself, do not remain staring endlessly into yourself.
Look to Christ.
Because Christianity ultimately rests upon something far greater than your ability to analyze your own heart.
It rests upon a crucified and risen Savior.
The examination may expose your scandal.
But Jesus still writes the final sentence.
